note: Proposed, not sealed. Written by the willow fleet seat while closing the T1-nestor-canon bite of the fleet loop plan (a survey-driven wave fixing stale canon across the fleet, not a feature). Three small findings, one shape: a fact declared once somewhere in the tree and repeated by hand somewhere else, with nothing checking the repeat still agreed.

decisions.question: nestor/serve.py's SERVER_VERSION was a hand-typed literal ("0.1.0") frozen since an early release while the package moved to 0.20.0 through hatch-vcs. Should the MCP server report its own version, or the package's?
decisions.commitment: The package's. SERVER_VERSION = __version__ (nestor/__init__.py's own derived value, imported alongside the other package submodules serve.py already imports from `.`). The MCP server has no release cadence independent of the nestor-meaning distribution — it ships inside the same wheel and moves with every tag — so a second number was never tracking anything real, only going stale. tests/test_the_version_is_written_once's rule ("nothing tracked in this tree may carry the version literal") is now enforced tree-wide, not just for nestor/__init__.py's own __version__: test_no_version_literal_hides_anywhere_under_nestor in tests/test_version.py scans every nestor/*.py file for a *VERSION*-named assignment holding a semver-shaped string literal, with no name exempted. If a genuinely independent server/protocol revision is ever needed, it gets its own constant, its own name, and its own line in that test's exemption set — argued for by name, not defaulted into reusing SERVER_VERSION.
decisions.why: A model-facing MCP client reads serverInfo.version to decide what the server can do; a version 19 releases behind is a lie a client could act on, and nothing had ever re-derived it because nothing checked. The general rule (test_the_version_is_written_once) already existed for the one place a version is supposed to live; the gap was that it only looked at nestor/__init__.py, so a second literal anywhere else in the package was invisible to it. Widening the scan rather than adding a second, serve.py-specific test keeps the rule one mechanism: any future *VERSION* name anywhere under nestor/ is caught the same way, not by remembering to add a bespoke check per module.

decisions.question: .pre-commit-config.yaml pinned ruff at v0.15.0 while scripts/lint-pins.txt and pyproject.toml's [dev] extra had both already moved to 0.16.6 (agent-log §6.114/§6.119 record exactly this shape of drift, for the same tool, one level up). Should the pre-commit pin be corrected once, or should something read it going forward?
decisions.commitment: Both. The pin is corrected to v0.16.6 now, and scripts/lint-pins-check.sh (already the single place that compares the local environment's tool versions against lint-pins.txt) reads .pre-commit-config.yaml's ruff-pre-commit rev too and refuses on disagreement, with the mismatch reported in the same voice as its existing checks ("this environment has X, CI pins Y"). A pre-commit hook running a different ruff from ci-lint.sh and CI is a gate disagreeing with the one branch protection runs, which is the exact failure lint-pins.txt was created to close for pip-installed tools — a hook pin is the same fact, held a third way, and had no guard.
decisions.why: The correction alone would have drifted again on the next ruff bump exactly as it already had once; lint-pins.txt already exists as the one file both ci-lint.sh and the workflow read from; extending its checker to a third reader (pre-commit) rather than inventing a parallel check keeps "one file, two callers, neither keeping its own copy" (the pattern secret-scan.sh and dep-audit.sh already follow) true of a third caller instead of carving out an exception for it.

decisions.question: README.md and docs/project-layout.md each summarize IDEAS.md's status vocabulary in one line as "measured / verified / hypothesis / open" — four tags. IDEAS.md's own status table lists exactly those four; a fifth, shipped, is introduced in the paragraph immediately after the table ("mark it **shipped**") and is, by count in the Map, the single most common tag (roughly 60 of 170 entries). Is the four-tag summary wrong, and if so what stops it drifting back?
decisions.commitment: Wrong, and fixed to name all five in both places. A new test, tests/test_docs.py::test_readme_and_layout_name_every_ideas_status_tag, reads IDEAS.md's table and its shipped-sentence as the one source of the vocabulary (not a hardcoded tuple duplicated three ways) and asserts both summaries reproduce it exactly, tag for tag, in order.
decisions.why: A status vocabulary is only useful if a reader can trust the doc that describes it; a summary that silently drops the tag most entries carry teaches a narrower, wrong reading of IDEAS.md to anyone who reads the front door instead of the source. The table itself was not touched — shipped genuinely lives in prose below it, by IDEAS.md's own design (§6's rule folds shipped substance back into the numbered section rather than growing the table), so the fix is not "add a row" but "read the whole declared vocabulary, table plus the sentence that extends it," and hold both summaries to that, not to the table alone.
